blocks.text: Words into algebra: a tutor's kit

Sam can solve an equation once it is written down. The hard part is the step before: turning a sentence into the equation. This kit gives you five ways to show that step, three routes to fit the time you have, and a pause built in before every example so Sam explains before writing.

blocks.title: Pick your route before you start
blocks.body: You never have to do it all. Each route is complete on its own and ends with the next-time note, so the following session picks up where this one stopped.

items: Quick route: the translation strip together, Example 1 (the number machine), then the quiz until Sam gets three right in a row. Make the note.
Standard route: the Quick route, then Example 2 (the balance) and Example 3 (shirt numbers), then Build the equation.
Deep route: all five examples, Words to symbols, Solve it in order, the full quiz, and Sam's own sentence at the end.

blocks.title: The fast path
blocks.body: If Sam gets the first three quiz questions right first time, skip Examples 1 and 2 and go straight to Example 4 (the pitch). If Sam misses two in a row, drop back to the balance: it shows what an equation means, and the rest follows from it.

blocks.title: The translation strip (keep this in view)
blocks.body: more than, altogether, in total: add. less than, fewer than, difference: take away, and watch the order: 5 less than x is x - 5, never 5 - x. times, twice, each: multiply. shared equally, half of, divided by: divide. is, makes, costs the same as: the equals sign.

blocks.text: Sam is around 15 or 16, working at O-level standard. Sam can add, subtract, multiply and divide with negatives, expand a simple bracket, and solve an equation like 3x + 4 = 19 when it is already written down.

Sentences are where it breaks. The words come in an order that is not the order of the algebra ("5 less than x"), a bracket hides inside a phrase ("twice the sum of"), and a sentence often describes the same thing twice ("together", "the same as"). This kit takes those three traps one at a time.

blocks.title: The pause is the method
blocks.body: Before each example, Sam reads the sentence and says it back in plain words: what is unknown, and what is the same as what. Then you wait. The silence feels long, and it is where the understanding happens. If you are short of time, cut an example, not the pause.

blocks.do: Example 1, the number machine. Sam says the sentence back, then runs the machine backwards with the Undo buttons.
blocks.say: Tell me in your own words what we don't know. Then: if we undo the machine, what comes off first?
blocks.why: Undoing the last step first is the whole idea of solving. The machine makes the order visible. Short of time: this example alone carries the Quick route.

blocks.do: Example 2, the balance. Sam takes the same thing off both sides until one scarf is on its own.
blocks.say: What is the same as what in this sentence? Show me on the scale.
blocks.why: "Costs the same as" is the equals sign. The balance never tips, so Sam sees that every move must happen to both sides. If stuck: let Sam press the buttons and narrate each one.

blocks.do: Example 3, shirt numbers. Sam names the three numbers in terms of the smallest before writing anything.
blocks.say: If the smallest shirt is n, what are the next two called?
blocks.why: Consecutive means add 1 each time, not double. The bar model shows the extra 1 and 2 sitting on top of three equal bars. Short of time: skip to the quiz.

blocks.do: Example 4, the pitch: geometry and algebra together. Sam sketches the rectangle first and labels all four sides.
blocks.say: How many sides does a perimeter go round? Label every one before you add.
blocks.why: The classic slip is counting each side once. Four labelled sides on a sketch prevent it, and the bar model shows the two extra 30s.

blocks.do: Example 5, the tickets. Sam groups one ticket with its fee before multiplying.
blocks.say: What does one person pay altogether? Now how many people?
blocks.why: This is where brackets come from: the 4 multiplies the whole of (x + 3). The tiles show the four groups, then open them out.

blocks.title: What only you can do
items: Read Sam's face during the pause and know whether the silence is thinking or being stuck.
Wait a few seconds longer than feels comfortable before you help.
Praise the sentence Sam says back, not just the right answer.
Notice when a mistake is a reading problem rather than a maths problem.
Decide when to stop: end on something Sam got right.

blocks.title: Sam sets you a puzzle
blocks.body: At the end, Sam knows more about football than any worksheet. Ask Sam to make up a sentence about a real team, player or ticket price, and you turn it into an equation out loud while Sam checks you. Get one wrong on purpose and let Sam catch it.
blocks.prompt: You've seen five of mine. Give me one of yours, about anything in football, and I'll write the equation. Tell me if I get it wrong.

blocks.if: Sam writes 5 - x for "5 less than x"
blocks.then: Ask: which one is getting smaller? x is. So x comes first and 5 is taken from it: x - 5. Try "5 less than 20" with numbers first: 15, so 20 - 5.

blocks.if: Sam writes 2x + 3 for "twice the sum of x and 3"
blocks.then: Ask: what is being doubled, x, or the sum? The sum, so the sum is grouped first: 2(x + 3). Brackets are the word "sum" (or "each") made visible.

blocks.if: Sam writes x, 2x, 3x for consecutive numbers
blocks.then: Say three real shirt numbers in a row: 8, 9, 10. Is 10 three times 8? Each is one more, so n, n + 1, n + 2.

blocks.if: Sam adds only two sides for a perimeter
blocks.then: Draw the rectangle and walk a finger round it. Four sides, two of each length: 2w + 2(w + 30).

blocks.if: Sam writes only half the sentence ("t + 6 = 30")
blocks.then: Ask: who does the 30 belong to, one player or both? "Together" means both, so both go on the left.

blocks.if: Sam goes quiet and stops writing
blocks.then: Open the matching scene and let Sam press the buttons. Moving something is often easier than writing it.

blocks.q: What if Sam can already do all five?
blocks.a: Take the Deep route's last step straight away: Sam writes sentences for you. Writing a sentence from an equation is the same skill in reverse, and harder.

more.q: And if that is easy too?
more.a: Ask for a sentence that needs two unknowns, and stop there. That is the doorway to simultaneous equations, a good place to start next time.

more.q: Do I need to teach simultaneous equations now?
more.a: No. Note it in the next-time note; the next session is built from that.

blocks.q: What if time runs out mid-example?
blocks.a: Stop at the end of the pause, not in the middle of writing. Make the note: it records how far Sam got, so the next session starts there.

more.q: Should I finish the example for Sam?
more.a: No. An unfinished example Sam explained is worth more than a finished one you wrote. Leave it as the first thing next time.

blocks.title: Reskin it for your learner
blocks.body: Everything here is built through football, but the mechanics do not depend on it. Give MetaDAX your next learner's interest (music, horses, gaming in plain words, cooking) and the same five examples, scenes and games come back in their world. Copy the line below into the MetaDAX prompt or skill.

blocks.title: To rebuild this for another learner
blocks.text: Build a MetaDAX tutor kit on turning sentences into algebra for a learner aged about 15 at O-level standard. Use the five worked examples (number machine, balance, consecutive numbers, perimeter, brackets with tickets) and the same games, but build every sentence through what this learner loves: [their interest]. Keep the three routes and the say-it-back pause before each example.
Tick what happened, add a line in your own words, and make the note. It already knows how the games went. Paste it in next time and the next session is built from it.

blocks.title: How did it go?
items: Sam said each sentence back before writing

blocks.title: You are the football expert
blocks.body: You know more about football than this page does. At the end you will make up a sentence about a real team or ticket price, and your tutor turns it into algebra. Your job is to check it.
blocks.prompt: Think of one now: a score, a price, a number of fans.

blocks.text: Algebra is just a sentence written in signs. x is the number we don't know yet. Before every example, say the sentence back in your own words. Take your time: that is the most important step.

blocks.title: Words to symbols
blocks.intro: Put each phrase in the box for the sign it means.

items.why: Altogether means add the parts up.
5 less than x is x - 5. Watch the order.
Two sides that cost the same are equal.

blocks.text: Say it back first: what don't we know, and what does the machine do to it?

blocks.title: Example 1: the number machine
blocks.ask_learner: Double last season's goals, then add 5 cup goals, and you get 23. How many goals last season? Undo the machine to find out.
blocks.why: 2x + 5 = 23. Undo the + 5 first: 2x = 18. Then undo the doubling: x = 9.

blocks.text: Say it back first: what is the same as what?

blocks.title: Example 2: the balance
blocks.ask_learner: Two scarves and a 4 pound badge cost the same as one scarf and an 11 pound programme. How many pounds is one scarf?
blocks.why: 2x + 4 = x + 11. Take one scarf off both sides: x + 4 = 11. Take 4 off both sides: x = 7.

blocks.text: Say it back first: if the smallest number is n, what are the other two?

blocks.title: Example 3: shirt numbers
blocks.ask_learner: Three players have shirt numbers in a row. They add up to 72. What is the smallest shirt number?

blocks.text: Say it back first: how many sides does the perimeter go round?

blocks.title: Example 4: the pitch
blocks.ask_learner: A pitch is 30 m longer than it is wide. Its perimeter is 340 m. How many metres wide is it?

blocks.text: Say it back first: what does one person pay altogether?

blocks.title: Example 5: the tickets
blocks.ask_learner: Each ticket costs x pounds plus a 3 pound booking fee. Four tickets cost 56 pounds. What is x?
blocks.why: 4(x + 3) = 56. Open the brackets: 4x + 12 = 56. Take 12 away: 4x = 44. Share by 4: x = 11.

blocks.title: Build the equation
blocks.intro: Five fans each pay x pounds for a ticket and 2 pounds for a programme. Together they pay 70 pounds.

parts.label: What does one person pay?
parts.hint: A ticket and a programme, grouped.

blocks.explain: 5(x + 2) = 70. Share by 5: x + 2 = 14, so a ticket is 12 pounds.

blocks.title: Solve it in order
blocks.intro: Solve 3x + 7 = x + 19 the balance way: the same move to both sides each time.

mistakes.add-x: added x to both sides instead of taking it away
mistakes.take-2: took 2 away instead of sharing by 2

steps.label: Step 1
steps.prompt: Get the x's on one side.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.prompt: Get the numbers on the other side.

blocks.title: Say it in algebra
blocks.intro: Read the sentence, say it back to yourself, then pick the algebra that says the same thing.

reversed.name: put the two parts in the wrong order
reversed.guide: Wrote 5 - x for "5 less than x", or 5 / c for "c shared between 5". The words come in the opposite order to the algebra.

bracket.name: left out or misplaced the brackets
bracket.guide: Wrote 2x + 3 for "twice the sum of x and 3". The multiplier belongs to the whole group.

multiples.name: wrote consecutive numbers as multiples
multiples.guide: Wrote n, 2n, 3n instead of n, n + 1, n + 2.

once.name: counted each side of the perimeter once
once.guide: Added one width and one length instead of all four sides.

half.name: wrote only part of the sentence
half.guide: Turned one clause into algebra and dropped the rest, for example the "together".

wrongop.name: used the wrong operation for the words
wrongop.guide: Read "shared", "times" or "of" as the wrong sign.

items.q: 8 less than the number of fans, f

choices.msg: That one put the two parts in the wrong order. f is the one getting smaller, so f comes first.
Yes. f, with 8 taken away.
That one used the wrong operation for the words. "Less than" takes away.

items.q: Three times the goals, g, then 4 more

choices.msg: That one left out or misplaced the brackets. The 4 is added after the tripling, so no bracket.
That one used the wrong operation for the words. "Times" multiplies.
Yes. Triple first, then add 4.

items.hint: What happens first, the tripling or the adding?
items.explain: Three times g is 3g; 4 more makes 3g + 4.

items.q: A bill of c pounds shared equally between 5 friends

choices.msg: Yes. Shared equally means divide.
That one put the two parts in the wrong order. The bill is what gets shared, so c is on top.
That one used the wrong operation for the words. Shared equally divides.

items.hint: What is being shared, and into how many parts?

items.q: Half of the points, p, then 6 fewer

choices.msg: Yes. Halve first, then take 6.
That one put the two parts in the wrong order. The half is getting smaller, so it comes first.
That one used the wrong operation for the words. "Half of" divides by 2.

items.explain: Half of p is p/2; 6 fewer is p/2 - 6.

items.q: A striker scored 6 more goals than her teammate. Together they scored 30. The teammate scored t.

choices.msg: That one wrote only part of the sentence. "Together" means both players.
Yes. Teammate t, striker t + 6, together 30.
That one used the wrong operation for the words. "More than" adds.

items.q: Twice the sum of a number x and 3 is 26.

choices.msg: That one left out or misplaced the brackets. The whole sum is doubled.
That one used the wrong operation for the words. "Twice" multiplies.
Yes. The sum is grouped, then doubled.

items.q: Three shirt numbers in a row add up to 45. The smallest is n.

choices.msg: That one wrote consecutive numbers as multiples. Each is one more, not double.
Yes. One more each time.
That one wrote only part of the sentence. The +1 and +2 went missing.

items.hint: Say three real numbers in a row first.

items.q: A small goal frame is 1 m wider than it is tall. Its perimeter is 10 m. The height is h.

choices.msg: That one counted each side of the perimeter once. A frame has four sides.
That one left out or misplaced the brackets. Both widths are h + 1.
Yes. Two heights, two widths.

items.explain: 4h + 2 = 10, so h = 2: the frame is 2 m tall and 3 m wide.

items.q: A team has 5 fewer points than twice its rival's points, a. The team has 31.

choices.msg: Yes. Twice a, then 5 fewer.
That one put the two parts in the wrong order. Twice a is what gets smaller.
That one left out or misplaced the brackets. The 5 comes off after doubling.

items.q: A kit costs x pounds. Three kits cost the same as one kit and 40 pounds.

choices.msg: That one wrote only part of the sentence. The one kit on the other side went missing.
Yes. "The same as" is the equals sign.
That one used the wrong operation for the words. Three kits is 3 times x.

items.hint: What is the same as what?

items.q: Four season tickets at k pounds each, less a 20 pound discount, cost 360 pounds.

choices.msg: That one put the two parts in the wrong order. The tickets are what get the discount.
That one left out or misplaced the brackets. The discount is once, not on each ticket.
Yes. Four tickets, then 20 off once.

items.hint: Is the discount on each ticket, or once?

items.q: f fans are shared equally between 3 coaches. Then 12 more get on one coach, which now has 50.

choices.msg: Yes. Share first, then 12 more on one coach.
That one left out or misplaced the brackets. The 12 join after the sharing.
That one used the wrong operation for the words. Shared equally divides.

blocks.q: What if I can't see where to start?
blocks.a: Say the sentence back and find the word for equals: is, makes, the same as. Everything before it goes on one side.

more.a: Try it with a real number first. If x were 10, what would the sentence say? Then swap the 10 back for x.

more.q: What if I get it wrong?
more.a: Good. The page tells you which slip it was, so you know exactly what to fix next time.

blocks.text: Make up one sentence about football with a number you don't know. Say it to your tutor. They write the equation, and you check it.

ticks: Sam said each sentence back before writing

build.notes: Tutor kit, words into algebra, age 15-16, O-level standard. Football skin. Five worked examples on the four algebra scenes; routes Quick/Standard/Deep; say-it-back before each example.
